newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council readies approval for force for Albania.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council readies approval for force for Albania.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council may authorise as early as Friday a European-dominated force for Albania to guard deliveries of food and other necessities and help the country recover from violence and near-anarchy.
Council president Zbigniew Wlosowicz of Poland said members were working on a resolution that he believed "would be ready for adoption soon, hopefully for tonight (Friday)."
Several council members, after an informal session, said the vote would probably be taken late on Friday, or if this was not possible, on Saturday.
They said China still had strong reservations about U.N. approval of a regional force and might abstain, while Japan and Sweden wanted more details and precision on the mandate.
Italy, expected to lead and dominate the force, asked the council on Thursday to endorse the operation urgently and meet during the three-day holiday weekend.

Italian Ambassador Paolo Fulci, not a council member, circulated the resolution calling for authorisation for a "temporary and limited multinational force to facilitate the safe and prompt delivery of humanitarian assistance" and to help create a secure environment for that aid. France presented the document, now amended, to the council.
The force would have a three-month mandate.

Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular savings schemes collapsed, erasing millions of dollars. Rebels seized the south in March in an armed insurrection, blaming President Sali Berisha for the fiasco and demanding that he quit.

Since then gangs have roamed the south, stealing, looting, killing and creating a food crisis. On Thursday, 17 people died in a gun battle in Levan in central Albania in the country's most violent incident in the last two months.

The Italian proposal follows a Vienna meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which agreed to establish a civilian mission for the purpose of "providing advice and assistance" in democratization, the media, human rights and monitoring elections in June.
But the 54-nation body, reflecting divisions among its members, did not authorise foreign police or troops, saying the Security Council needed to give the mission a green light.
Asked why the OSCE was so hesitant, Fulci said, "Only the U.N. Security Council has a mandate for the whole international community. This is why it is important."
Seven Council members belong to the OSCE -- France, Britain, Russia and the United States, which are permanent members with veto power, as well as Sweden, Portugal and Poland.

Among those which have expressed willingness to send troops are France, Portugal, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Romania and Austria in addition to Italy. Britain, Germany and the United States will not send forces.

Italy has estimated about 2,500 personnel would be deployed initially, with another 2,500 in reserve. Albania wants foreign police or troops to help secure ports, airports, roads and railroads to ensure distribution of relief supplies.
Whether or not the troops guarding Albanian ports would prevent refugees from leaving is not clear.

Many Albanians have sought asylum in Italy, which on Monday decided to turn away boats heading towards southeast Italian ports across the Adriatic, a journey already made by some 12,000 people since March 13.

If authorised, diplomats said the status of the force would be similar to the U.S.-led operation to expel Iraqi troops from Kuwait or France's 1994 intervention. In both cases the United Nations gave the operations international legitimacy without organising the missions.
